title: 02. Tool Calling & MCP: Day 18 — Tool Ecosystems
summary: So far your agents have used one or two tools at a time. Today you build agents with rich tool ecosystems — six or more tools the agent must choose between, and tools that themselves invoke other LLMs.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body:
So far your agents have used one or two tools at a time. Today you build agents with **rich tool ecosystems** — six or more tools the agent must choose between, and tools that themselves invoke other LLMs. The challenge shifts from "how do I call a tool" to "how do I design tool surfaces the agent can navigate without confusion."

### Designing tool surfaces

A tool surface is everything the LLM sees about a tool: its name, parameter names and types, docstring, and return shape. As your tool count grows past five, the surface starts to matter more than the underlying implementation. Three rules of thumb. First, **names are verbs over nouns** (`read_email`, not `email_reader`): the LLM treats each tool as an action it can take, and verb-form names map cleanly to that mental model. Second, **docstrings are user manuals, not implementation notes**: the LLM cannot read your code, only your docstring. Write the docstring as if explaining the tool to a junior developer who will use it blind. Third, **return shapes should be small and structured**: a tool that returns a 50KB string will pollute the agent's context window for the rest of the run. Return only what the agent needs to decide the next step.

A common scaling question: how many tools can one agent handle? Empirically, modern models (GPT-4o, Claude 3.5) handle 10-15 tools reliably if their surfaces are well-designed; above that, accuracy drops and you should consider splitting into sub-agents (the multi-agent pattern from Day 15). The Inbox Zero Assistant below uses 7 tools, which is in the comfortable range. The Multi-doc Summarizer uses 4 tools but two of them internally invoke nested LLMs — a different scaling axis entirely.

Two projects. The first is an **Inbox Zero Assistant** in LangChain with six mock email tools plus `list_inbox`. The second is a **Multi-doc Summarizer** in Pydantic AI where `summarize_doc` and `merge_summaries` are tools that internally call nested LLM agents — the "agent-of-agents" pattern. The two projects illustrate the two scaling strategies: more tools (horizontal scale) and nested agents inside tools (vertical scale).

sections.title: Common Pitfalls
sections.body:
**Tool naming collisions.** If you name two tools `read` and `read_doc`, the LLM will sometimes call the wrong one. Use distinctive, verb-noun names: `read_email`, `read_doc`, `read_calendar_event`. Avoid single verbs (`read`, `get`, `list`) because they will collide as your tool set grows past 5.

**`max_iterations` too low.** With 7 tools and 5 emails, your agent may legitimately need 10-15 iterations. Set `max_iterations` generously for triage tasks (15-20) and tightly for single-action tasks (3-5). Watch the executor's "Stopped early" message — that means you hit the ceiling. Always log `result["output"]` to see what the agent managed to do before being cut off.

**Nested LLM costs multiplying silently.** A tool that calls an LLM inside another tool that calls an LLM can 100x your bill in a single user turn. Always count LLM calls in your head: outer agent + tool calls + nested agent calls. For the Multi-doc Summarizer, 4 docs = 1 (outer) + 4 (summarize_doc) + 1 (theme_extractor) + 1 (final response) = 7 calls. Set per-request cost ceilings with `model_settings={"max_tokens": 500}` on nested agents.

**Tools returning huge strings.** If `read_doc` returns a 50,000-character document, that text goes into the outer agent's context window — and now the outer agent is reading the whole doc instead of delegating. Keep tool outputs short. For long docs, return a truncated preview plus a `summarize_doc` tool the agent can call separately. This pattern keeps the outer agent's context lean.

**Forgetting `handle_parsing_errors`.** Even with tool calling, models occasionally emit malformed tool calls. `AgentExecutor(handle_parsing_errors=True)` recovers gracefully by feeding the error back to the model with a "please try again" message. Without this, one bad tool call crashes the whole run. For Pydantic AI, the equivalent is automatic retries on validation failures (configured via `model_settings`).
